newsitem.title: THAILAND: U.S. sanctions on Burma spark fears of retaliation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sanctions on Burma spark fears of retaliation.

text.p: A U.S. decision to impose sanctions on Burma raises the questions of what Rangoon will do now and whether sanctions will help or hurt human rights in the impoverished Southeast Asian country, analysts said on Tuesday.

Some diplomats and businessmen said the sanctions, sparked by reports of rights abuses by the military government, may backfire and the generals may end up clamping down further on opposition democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
"The question we have to ask now is how will they retaliate," said a Rangoon-based diplomat.

The State Department will officially announce the sanctions banning new U.S. investment in Burma later on Tuesday, Washington officials said. The sanctions have already been approved by President Bill Clinton.

"What will the SLORC do? Will they direct their retaliation against the U.S. or will they move against Aung San Suu Kyi and the opposition?" the diplomat said, referring to the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council.
SLORC has been accused by human rights organisations, the United Nations and many western governments of human rights violations such as summary executions, forced labour and rape.
It has also been condemned for failing to recognise the landslide 1990 electoral victory of the National League for Democracy (NLD), which was co-founded and now led by Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi.
The U.S. sanctions were approved by the Senate late last year following a series of crackdowns on Suu Kyi and the NLD.
Thousands of NLD supporters were detained last year, and Suu Kyi was put under virtual house arrest in December following rare student demonstrations in Rangoon.
Suu Kyi, who was under official house arrest for six years for her outspoken attacks on the government, has publicly supported sanctions and urged foreigners not to invest in Burma.
There was no official reaction from Burma on Tuesday, but a government spokesman told Reuters that SLORC was more concerned about Burma than was the United States or any other nation.

"If the U.S. is so genuinely concerned about the human rights of the Myanmar (Burma) people, why is it so necessary to deprive one of the most essential rights of the Myanmar people -- the right to earn a living and support the family?" he said.
Last week a Burmese government official said U.S. sanctions were liked a weapon aimed at destroying the rights of Burmese people to earn a decent living and support their family.
Some diplomats said SLORC was likely to retaliate soon.
"It depends on how much this has taken them by surprise, since sanctions have been on the cards for some time," one said.
In the past, SLORC has reacted in kind when faced with restrictions by western governments but the poor country clearly lacks international economic and political clout.
When the United States and the European Union issued visa restrictions on SLORC officials last year, Rangoon slapped similar restrictions on officials from those nations.
Some diplomats said SLORC may be wary of making any major moves while Burma awaits full membership in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Burma, Cambodia and Laos are expected to be admitted to the seven-nation group this year, possibly in July.

International prressure has mounted on ASEAN not to admit Burma but ASEAN follows a "constructive engagement" policy and has in the past said it will not interfere into the politics of another nation.
"But this could put pressure on ASEAN to really decide which way they want to go," one diplomat said.

Oil and gas company Unocal Corp is the largest American investor in Burma, helping to make the United States the fourth largest foreign investor in the country in terms of approved foreign investment.
Unocal chairman Roger Beach told a business luncheon earlier on Tuesday that sanctions were counterproductive, and hurt people not regimes.

"In numerous countries, sanctions have had the effect of hurting the poor the most," he told the American Chamber of Commerce. "Sanctions...hurt people. And they cut off American companies from places in the world where we should be involved."
